- If sentiment is consistently negative or low (e.g., < 0.2) over recent days, model tends to overestimate; reduce forecast slope or shift downward.
- If sentiment spikes upward (e.g., > 0.7) and model continues rising, check for overshoot — cap forecast at 1–2% above recent peak if sentiment is strong.
- When true outcome shows sharp downward correction after a spike, model often lags — adjust forecast to reflect earlier reversal if sentiment turns negative.
- If model forecast is rising steadily but true outcome shows mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 consecutive days of decline), reduce forecast slope or add downward bias.
- If sentiment is neutral or mixed (0.3–0.7) and model is trending upward, consider adding a 1–3% downward adjustment to avoid overconfidence.
- If model forecast is flat or slightly rising but true outcome shows strong volatility, reduce forecast smoothness — allow ±2% deviation from recent mean for sentiment-driven swings.
- If sentiment history shows recent negative sentiment (e.g., 3+ days < 0.2) and model is still rising, apply a “sentiment correction” — subtract 0.5–1.5% from forecast for next 3–5 days.
- If model forecast is significantly above true outcome (e.g., > 5% over 3–5 days), check for sentiment lag — if sentiment is rising, model may be overreacting; reduce forecast by 1–2% per day until sentiment stabilizes.
